title: Ten years of Mapping Museums
paragraphs: It is ten years ago this month that the first Mapping Museums project started. In September 2016, Alexandra Poulovassilis, Jamie Larkin, and I began the process of collecting, modelling, and analysing data on the UK museums sector since 1960. Andrea Ballatore soon joined, bringing expertise in geography and data analysis. Since then, the team has grown, and we’ve completed three major projects. I want to take a moment to think about what we’ve achieved and what is left to do.

The Mapping Museums database showed that the UK museum sector was bigger and more varied than assumed, and it made non-national museums, and especially local authority and independent museums more visible within the sector than had previously been the case. It was also the first time that non-accredited museums had been documented. When the database first launched in 2020, Lisa Ollerhead (Senior policy advisor for museums at the Department of Digital, Culture, Media and Sport and now director of the Association of Independent Museums) called it ‘a game changer’, because it provided reliable data on the size and composition of the UK museum sector. That information has since been used by numerous governmental and non-governmental agencies in their research for policy and funding bids.

The launch of the database exactly coincided with the start of the Covid pandemic and, concerned that the numbers of museum closures might escalate, we started work on our second project ‘UK Museums in the Pandemic‘. Andrea and Jamie worked with Peter Wood, Valeri Katerinchuk, Ekaterina Mityurova, and Mark Liebenrood, to map patterns of temporary and permanent closures using web-scraping technologies. Perhaps counter-intuitively the number of closures was lower during the pandemic than in previous years.

Our most recent project also took closure as its subject. In ‘Museum Closure in the UK 2000-25’ we investigated why museums had closed and what happened to the collections. We collected data, George Wright built a software application to analyse and visualise that information, and streamlined the existing Mapping Museums database, and we released the new combined database with an accompanying report in December 2025. Like the first Mapping Museums project, ‘Museum Closure’ breaks new ground. It documents museum closure at a national scale for the first time, drawing attention to the churn (the degree of opening and closing) in the UK sector, the varied reasons for closure, and the subsequent flows of objects.

Throughout the three research projects we have published articles on methods: on devising workable definitions of museums, managing patchy data, developing agile technologies to map changing data, and using large language models to monitor change. We have also published findings with articles concentrating on the changing composition of the museum sector, the geography of the UK museum sector, the pivot to social media during the pandemic, and the movement of collections after museums close, among other subjects. Many of these topics were discussed in even greater detail in the dozens of blogs we published on our work in progress.

The projects have also generated two monographs. Stories From Small Museums, by Fiona Candlin, Toby Butler and Jake Watts, drew on interviews with museum founders to ask why individuals and groups were motivated to start their own museums, and was published to good reviews. Oliver Betts, curator at the National Transport Museum wrote that ‘I can scarcely remember a book that I discussed more frequently with colleagues in the museum, often a group who struggle to find time for reading museum studies. It is an important intervention in the field (and) a reminder for those of us already working in the sector of why we do what we do, and how special it can be for those who participate’. The second book Closed Museums is due out next year. And finally, the projects have resulted in two archival resources. Bishopsgate Institute Library and Archive has published our interviews with founders as the ‘Mapping Museums Oral Histories’ and Mark worked with the British Library to create the ‘Closed Museums’ web archive, which will be publicly available in the coming months.

The three projects completed, we are now looking at ways of securing the future of the database and to ensure that we can continue to provide up-to-date information on the changing shape of the UK museum sector. While we have benefitted from generous academic grants, this funding only covers the creation of the database and not its maintenance. I hope to keep you posted on future developments.
Fiona Candlin
September 2026
Photo by Annie Spratt

title: Archiving websites about closed museums
paragraphs: When we launched our report on museum closure last December, the British Library approached us to ask if we would be interested in using our research as the basis for a website archive.

It seemed a very appropriate project to get involved in. Websites have often proved to be invaluable sources for information about museums – not only for those that are open, of course, but also for those that have closed. Online resources have provided data for all three projects that the Mapping Museums Lab has undertaken, but our most recent project on museum closure highlighted once again a problem that’s well known by those that undertake research online.

For our first project, Mapping Museums, we recorded the sources of information for each museum, which frequently included websites. When we checked some of those again for our latest project six years later, many of those sites had gone offline. This phenomenon, known as ‘link rot’, is all too common and services have been developed to deal with the issue by archiving as much of the internet as possible. Probably the best known of these is the Wayback Machine at the Internet Archive. Wayback has proved invaluable for tracking down extinct websites, or single pages removed from a site that’s still online.

The UK Web Archive fulfils a similar purpose for UK websites. It’s a partnership of the six UK Legal Deposit Libraries – including the British Library – and aims to collect as much as possible of the UK’s web space. The archive began on a selective basis in 2005 and scaled up from 2013 onwards. The collection contains millions of websites and new ones are being added all the time. Due to the cyber-attack in November 2023, the archive is currently unavailable but the work of collecting websites continues.

With so many websites in existence, how to choose what to archive? The British Library’s archivists rely partly on nominations from the public to make their choices and this is where Mapping Museums comes in. We are contributing a thematic collection of websites that have provided information about museum closure. Some of these belonged to the museums themselves, but more commonly the site fulfils a different purpose.

We’ve used a wide variety of sources. News websites are probably the most common, and those of museums and related bodies like the Museums Association, but we also consulted auction houses, estate agents, listed building records, review websites (e.g. Tripadvisor), Government and local authorities, local history groups and specialist societies, hospitals, universities, heritage organisations such as the National Trust, personal websites, discussion forums, the Historic Ships Register, heritage railways, and more besides.

Work is underway on nominating a long list of websites like these from our previous research. Revisiting them just a few years later, we’re already finding that some have gone offline entirely or individual pages have been removed. Fortunately some sites are already in the UK Web Archive, but this is not true for all of them. As link rot continues, that makes this mini archiving project all the more relevant. We’re very happy to be supporting the long-term preservation of online resources that we’ve often found invaluable when researching the histories of hundreds of museums in the UK.
Mark Liebenrood

title: Museums and the Promise of Permanence
paragraphs: Thursday 14th May 2026, 4pm, The Conservatory, Birkbeck, Malet Street, London

The International Council for Museums defines museums as ‘permanent institutions’, as does the UK Museums Association. This seminar critically addresses the aspiration to permanence, its value, and its limits. We ask what would museums be if not permanent?
Speakers:
Bruno Brulon Soares ‘Permanence and Precarity’
Fiona Candlin ‘At Stake in Permanence’
Chair: Bethany Rex
Tickets are free but please a book a place

Bethany Rex, Research Fellow, Centre for Cultural & Media Policy Studies, University of Warwick. Following doctoral work on local government and museum asset transfer, Bethany has researched museum closures, decision-making in local government and how the commercialisation of museums is being experienced by museum staff. She is currently working on a book about museum closures (MUP, 2028).

Bruno Brulon Soares, Reader in Museum and Heritage Studies in the School of Art History, University of St Andrews. Between 2020 and 2022, Bruno was co-Chair of the Standing Committee for the Museum Definition (ICOM Define) and coordinated the global participatory project that led to the approval of a new museum definition adopted by the International Council of Museums in August 2022. He is the author of The Anticolonial Museum (Routledge 2024) and co-author of The Museum Definition Handbook (ICOM, 2025) with Lauran Bonilla-Merchav.

Fiona Candlin, Professor of Museology. School of Historical Studies, Birkbeck, University of London. Fiona is Director of the Mapping Museums Lab, a multi-disciplinary research group that has documented and analysed the history and development of the UK museum sector since 1960. Their most recent project addresses closure. She is author of Art, Museums and Touch (MUP 2009); Micromuseology (Bloomsbury 2015); Stories from Small Museums (MUP 2022) and many articles, chapters, and reports. She has almost finished a new book provisionally called Closed Museums and After.

title: Major Changes to the Mapping Museums Lab Database
paragraphs: We’re delighted to announce that key functions from the original Mapping Museums Lab database have now been fully integrated into our new web application.

We are very grateful to Art Fund for helping fund additional development work, which has enabled us to extend and strengthen the Mapping Museums Lab resource for the benefit of the wider museums and heritage community.

This update brings together, in one place, the rich data from our first major project — a comprehensive database of all museums open in the UK from 1960 to the present — with our second major strand of research: detailed information on museums that have closed, including reasons for closure and the outcomes for their collections. For the first time, users can seamlessly explore all the Mapping Museums Lab data in one site.
Responding to input from our sector evaluation sessions, the addition to the web application offers a more flexible and intuitive user experience. You can now:

Search for individual museums using free text
View detailed information for each museum
Generate and search across lists of all museums in the database
We’ve also refreshed and expanded our accreditation data. Records have been updated and accreditation numbers added, making it easier to track institutional status and align our data with other resources and sector standards.

Whether you’re a researcher, policymaker, sector professional, or independent scholar, the new platform is designed to make the data more discoverable, usable, and interconnected than ever before. We look forward to seeing how you use it.
The original Mapping Museums database will no longer be updated.

title: New article on museum closure data
paragraphs: The Mapping Museums Lab has just published an article in the Journal of Open Humanities Data about our project on museum closure. If you are interested in finding out more about how we collected and managed the data, the article is open access and free for everyone to read: A Dataset of Collections Dispersal Following Museum Closures in the UK During 2000–2025.
